verses.text: These are the words of Agur son of Jakeh—the burden that this man declared to Ithiel: "I am weary, O God, and worn out.
Surely I am the most ignorant of men, and I lack the understanding of a man.
I have not learned wisdom, and I have no knowledge of the Holy One.

Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in His hands? Who has bound up the waters in His cloak? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is His name, and what is the name of His Son— surely you know!
Every word of God is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him.
Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar.
Two things I ask of You— do not refuse me before I die:
Keep falsehood and deceitful words far from me. Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion.
Otherwise, I may have too much and deny You, saying, 'Who is the LORD?' Or I may become poor and steal, profaning the name of my God.
Do not slander a servant to his master, or he will curse you, and you will bear the guilt.
There is a generation of those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers.
There is a generation of those who are pure in their own eyes and yet unwashed of their filth.
There is a generation—how haughty are their eyes and pretentious are their glances—
there is a generation whose teeth are swords and whose jaws are knives, devouring the oppressed from the earth and the needy from among men.
The leech has two daughters: Give and Give. There are three things that are never satisfied, four that never say, 'Enough!':
Sheol, the barren womb, land never satisfied with water, and fire that never says, 'Enough!'
As for the eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother, may the ravens of the valley pluck it out and young vultures devour it.
There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot understand:
the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a snake on a rock, the way of a ship at sea, and the way of a man with a maiden.
This is the way of an adulteress: She eats and wipes her mouth and says, 'I have done nothing wrong.'
Under three things the earth trembles, under four it cannot bear up:
a servant who becomes king, a fool who is filled with food,
an unloved woman who marries, and a maidservant who supplants her mistress.
Four things on earth are small, yet they are exceedingly wise:
The ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in the summer;
the rock badgers are creatures of little power, yet they make their homes in the rocks;
the locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation;
and the lizard can be caught in one's hands, yet it is found in the palaces of kings.
There are three things that are stately in their stride, and four that are impressive in their walk:
a lion, mighty among beasts, refusing to retreat before anything;
a strutting rooster; a he-goat; and a king with his army around him.
If you have foolishly exalted yourself or if you have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth.
For as the churning of milk yields butter, and the twisting of the nose draws blood, so the stirring of anger brings forth strife."

context.author: Agur son of Jakeh (30:1), otherwise unknown. His words may come from Massa, a tribe of north Arabia (Genesis 25:14), if that is what the Hebrew word massa means here.
context.genre: Wisdom poetry: a confession, a prayer and numbered sayings
context.audience: Ithiel (30:1), and every reader humbled before God
context.mapLabel: THE WORDS OF AGUR, PLACE UNKNOWN
context.setting: “These are the words of Agur son of Jakeh” (v.1), a man nobody else in the Bible mentions. He begins humbly: “I am weary, O God, and worn out… I have no knowledge of the Holy One” (vv.1-3). Then he asks a string of questions: “Who has ascended to heaven and come down?… What is His name, and what is the name of His Son— surely you know!” (v.4). Every word of God is flawless (v.5). His prayer asks for two things: keep lies far away, and “give me neither poverty nor riches” (vv.7-9). The rest of the chapter is numbered sayings, built on the pattern three things, and four: things never satisfied (vv.15-16), things too wonderful to understand (vv.18-19), things the earth cannot bear (vv.21-23), four small but very wise creatures (vv.24-28), and four that move with stately grace (vv.29-31).
context.custom: The Hebrew word massa in v.1 (BSB “the burden”) can mean an oracle, or it can be the name of Massa, a tribe descended from Ishmael that lived in north Arabia (Genesis 25:14). If so, Agur may not have been an Israelite, yet he speaks of Israel’s God. The rock badger (v.26) is the rock hyrax, a small animal that lives in rocky cliffs in Israel. Locusts swarm in vast armies with no king (v.27), and small geckos climb the walls of palaces (v.28).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 31 gives the words of King Lemuel’s mother and the poem of the noble wife.
context.timelineBible: Agur’s questions (v.4) echo God’s questions to Job (Job 38:4-11). Verse 5 is close to Psalm 18:30 and 2 Samuel 22:31, and v.6 to Deuteronomy 4:2. Jesus answers v.4 in John 3:13: “No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven— the Son of Man” (John 3:13). His prayer for daily bread (Matthew 6:11) is like v.8.

translation.meaning: A name meaning perhaps “gatherer.” Later Jewish tradition took it as a name for Solomon, but the text presents a different man.
Refined, tested in fire. Every word of God has been tested and found pure.
An allotted share. “Feed me with the bread that is my portion”: enough for today.

gospelParallels.note: No one has ascended into heaven except the One who came down.
Give us this day our daily bread (v.8).
If we have food and clothing, we will be content.

otBackground.note: Where were you when I laid the earth’s foundations?
The word of the LORD is flawless; he is a shield.

overview.summary: Agur confesses his ignorance, asks who made the world and what is His Son’s name, prays for neither poverty nor riches, and gives numbered sayings about wonders in creation.
overview.settingLine: A humble teacher, perhaps from north Arabia.

history.t: An Ishmaelite tribe in north Arabia.
The East was famous for wisdom (1 Kings 4:30).

customs.t: Three things, and four: a way to make listeners think.
Bloodsucking worms in pools and streams.

archaeology.t: The oasis of Tayma in north Arabia has inscriptions from the age of the kings of Judah.
Hyraxes still live in the cliffs of Ein Gedi.

overview.discussion: Agur prays, “Give me neither poverty nor riches” (v.8). Why might having too much be as dangerous as having too little?
overview.book: The book of Proverbs · 31 chapters. Short sayings and longer poems that teach how to live wisely in God’s world, beginning with the fear of the LORD.
overview.author: Agur son of Jakeh

peoplePlaces.n: The ant, hyrax, locust and lizard

historicalImage.caption: Harvester ants (Messor) carrying seeds into their nest. Agur names the ant first among four small, wise creatures: “they store up their food in the summer” (Proverbs 30:25).

currentImage.caption: Storage jars of the kind that held the Dead Sea Scrolls. Two fragmentary copies of Proverbs (4Q102 and 4Q103) were among the scrolls found near Qumran.
